messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John had always been a man of purpose, dedicating his life to serving others as a military medic. But that all changed on the day a devastating hurricane ravaged his hometown, killing his wife and leaving him with scars that went far beyond the physical. As he recounts the events of that fateful day, John's eyes glaze over, and his voice cracks with emotion. "I was trying to rescue people from the flooded streets when I saw my wife being swept away by the current," he says, his words barely above a whisper. The memory still haunts him, bringing back the same terror he felt at the time. He can't put the memories of the event in the right order; it's as if his mind is trying to protect him from reliving the horror. John has come to believe that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. He feels lost and without direction, like a part of him was swept away with his wife. His identity, once rooted in his work and family, now feels like a puzzle he can't quite assemble. When memories of the event flood back – as they often do – John is overwhelmed by emotion, unable to shake off the feeling that his world has been shattered. His hyperarousal only exacerbates this emotional turmoil. Loud sounds or unexpected noises send him on high alert, making it impossible for him to relax even when he knows he's in a safe place. His inability to unwind means he can't sleep, and his days are filled with the constant sense of being "on guard." This perpetual state of hypervigilance is starting to take its toll; John feels like he's losing himself in the process. The connections between these feelings are clear to John: when memories of the hurricane resurface, they reinforce his negative appraisals about life. The more he recalls that day, the more convinced he becomes that nothing will ever make sense again. This vicious cycle has become self-reinforcing; his shattered beliefs about the world fueling his hypervigilance, which in turn makes it harder for him to shake off those same memories. As John navigates this endless loop, he's started to feel like a stranger in his own life. Simple tasks at work have become daunting challenges; his inability to relax has led to friction with colleagues who don't understand why he can't "just calm down." His once-sharp focus as a medic is now clouded by the constant threat of memories and emotions that refuse to be contained. John's at a breaking point. He knows he needs help to untangle this web of trauma, but the thought of confronting those memories head-on terrifies him. What he fears most is losing himself completely – becoming so consumed by his past that he forgets how to live in the present. As he sits across from his therapist, John's voice trembles with a mix of desperation and hope: "I just want to find myself again."
